newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Tietmeyer says dlr rise should end, Europe a factor.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says dlr rise should end, Europe a factor.

text.p: German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in an interview to be broadcast in Hungary next week that he was against any further rise in the dollar against the mark, which he said was caused in part by criticism of European integration.

"We are not interested that the mark should be devalued (further)," he said. "The recent rise was only a correction process but we are not interested in a correction process that would go beyond tolerable limits."
Tietmeyer told Hungarian Radio the level of the mark against the dollar was currently "absolutely correct".
The dollar stood at 1.69 marks on most markets at the time of the interview on Monday.
"The development of a currency rate with a stronger dollar is to a large extent a correction of an exaggerated development of the past," he said.
"Of course we are not interested in an overvalued currency but we are interested that the mark should be valued correctly and we have the impression that the value of the mark is all right now."

Tietmeyer was speaking in an interview given to Hungarian Radio in Franfurt which is to be broadcast to coincide with the arrival in Hungary next Tuesday of German president Roman Herzog for a three-day visit.
A copy of the recording was obtained by Reuters
The Bundesbank president said criticism of future European integration was a factor in the dollar's recent rise.
A number of European politicians have expressed doubts recently that the January 1, 1999 deadline for the single European currency will be met.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday that on balance his government was hostile to a single currency for the European Union.
"It could be the case that in the present development one or the other critical attitude towards European development is a factor included (in the dollar's rise)," Tietmeyer said.
The Bundesbank President said a cut in the German central bank's interest rates was unlikely in the short term.
"We shall follow very carefully the monetary figures which for the time being are too expansionist and therefore in the short term a further fall in interest rates is not likely," he said.

"The monetary conditions for growth are given because the interest rates are lower than ever before. We have the central bank interest rates at a record low, we have the capital market interest rates also at a record low, so on the monetary side the preconditions are given for new growth."
However Tietmeyer did not rule out adjustments to interest rates later in 1997.

"We regularly examine whether the present interest rate policy should remain or should be changed and I dont see any reason for a change in the foreseable future, particularly upwards, but I cannot exclude in the course of the year that changes occur."
However, sustainable growth could only be achieved by taking tough decisions in order to get the current high level of Germen unemployment down and investment up, he said.

"The present unemployment is depressingly high and everything has to be done to push it sustainably down," he said. "But there is no ready recipe but there are some very important decisions for example over tax regulations, social legislation and wage level agreements."

"What is at stake is Germany's long-term competitiveness in a changing world," he said. "We need enough internal flexibility because the economic structure is changing and therefore labour forces have to adapt...their readiness for mobility and flexibility."
He said such changes in attitude would take time.
"It is a solution which can be reached only in the course of several years but the decision for this is urgent and important."

Tietmeyer predicted that the creation of the single European currency along with the planned enlargement of the European Union would result in a future EU structure of three concentric circles according to how near states were to satisfying Maastricht criteria for monetary union.
"The European process in the coming decade will develop according to pattern of concentric circles," he said.

The first circle will include those few countries which will meet the requirements of monetary union by early next year, the second circle will contain the other member states, and the third Hungary and some advanced East Central European countries such as the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary and Slovenia, he said.
"But the circles have always to be open to new members," he added.
"I'm convinced that in 1999 and 200O the plans for a single European currency can be fulfilled," Tietmeyer said.
